clinicalPearls: Caused by direct or prolonged viewing of the sun, classically after solar eclipse gazing, sun worship, or telescope viewing without adequate filters, and increasingly reported after use of hallucinogens or psychiatric illness where sun-staring occurs.

Patients present hours to a day or two after exposure with bilateral (occasionally asymmetrical) central or paracentral scotoma, blurred vision, metamorphopsia, dyschromatopsia and sometimes chromatopsia or micropsia.
Visual acuity is often only mildly to moderately reduced despite marked symptomatic disturbance, and a positive history of sun exposure is the key to diagnosis.
Early fundus signs are subtle, a small yellow-white foveal spot, later evolving into a sharply defined reddish foveal lesion, and may be missed without careful stereoscopic macular examination.

Optical coherence tomography is the most sensitive investigation, characteristically showing a focal defect in the outer retinal layers at the fovea with disruption of the ellipsoid zone and interdigitation zone.
The injury is predominantly photochemical (and to a lesser extent thermal) damage to the photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium rather than a burn from focused heat alone.
Fluorescein angiography is often normal or shows only a subtle window defect, helping to distinguish it from exudative maculopathies.
No proven specific treatment exists; management centres on preventing further exposure, patient education and observation, with corticosteroids of unproven benefit.
reference.pathophysiology: Solar retinopathy results chiefly from photochemical injury to the outer retina when short-wavelength (blue) and near-ultraviolet light from direct solar viewing is focused by the optics of the eye onto the fovea. Absorbed radiant energy generates reactive oxygen species that damage photoreceptor outer segments and the underlying retinal pigment epithelium, with a smaller contribution from thermal energy that raises local tissue temperature. The fovea is preferentially affected because it lies at the point of optical focus and lacks the protective screening of inner retinal vasculature and, being cone-rich, is metabolically vulnerable. The acute insult produces oedema and disruption of the photoreceptor layer; over subsequent weeks the pigment epithelium and photoreceptors may partially recover or leave a permanent focal outer retinal defect, sometimes a small lamellar cavity, accounting for the residual scotoma. Predisposing factors include a clear atmosphere, dilated pupils, youth with clear ocular media, and pharmacological or behavioural states that prolong sun-gazing.
additionalDifferentials: Laser pointer or welding-arc phototoxic maculopathy
Macular hole or impending macular hole
Torpedo maculopathy or other focal outer retinal defect
additionalInvestigations: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the fovea for outer retinal and ellipsoid zone defects
Fundus autofluorescence to detect focal pigment epithelial change
Amsler grid testing to map the central scotoma and metamorphopsia
Fluorescein angiography to exclude exudative or inflammatory maculopathy
Microperimetry to quantify central sensitivity loss
Colour vision testing for acquired dyschromatopsia
Multifocal electroretinography in atypical or medicolegal cases
redFlags: History of prolonged or repeated unprotected sun-gazing suggesting cumulative bilateral injury
Persistent dense central scotoma beyond the expected recovery window indicating permanent foveal damage
Bilateral involvement threatening reading and driving vision
Underlying psychiatric illness or substance use driving compulsive sun-staring and re-injury
Progressive enlargement of the foveal defect suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Most patients experience partial or substantial recovery of visual acuity over weeks to months, though a small residual central or paracentral scotoma and subtle metamorphopsia frequently persist owing to the focal outer retinal defect. Prognosis is worse with more prolonged exposure, bilateral involvement or repeated injury.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because visual acuity is relatively preserved and early fundus findings are subtle, without eliciting the exposure history.
Mistaking the small foveal lesion for an early macular hole and pursuing surgical rather than conservative management.
Relying on ophthalmoscopy alone rather than obtaining optical coherence tomography, which is far more sensitive for the outer retinal defect.
Prescribing corticosteroids as if for an inflammatory maculopathy despite absence of proven benefit.
Neglecting to counsel on eye protection and address any underlying behavioural or psychiatric driver, risking recurrent phototoxic injury.
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Retina and Vitreous
management: There is no proven specific treatment; management is largely supportive observation, as visual acuity often recovers partially or substantially over weeks to months.
Remove ongoing exposure and counsel firmly against further sun-gazing.
A short course of corticosteroids is sometimes used, though evidence of benefit is limited.
Prevention through patient education, use of certified solar-eclipse filters, and addressing underlying drivers such as hallucinogen use or psychiatric illness prompting sun-staring.
Monitor recovery with optical coherence tomography of the fovea, visual acuity and Amsler grid mapping of the scotoma.
Refer to ophthalmology for confirmation, macular assessment and exclusion of other maculopathies.
